You pick your spot and your mind and senses are thoroughly engaged.
The irresistible score is similarly like nothing else on Broadway, to use an exhausted phrase that is in this case the simple truth.
The resulting music is irresistible to a totalitarian degree.

David Byrne and Fatboy Slim’s disco-infused extravaganza turns the theatre into a dance floor with thrilling results Let’s get the shoes out of the way. Here Lies Love, David Byrne and Fatboy Slim’s pop musical about Imelda Marcos, does not dwell on the kleptocrat’s notorious shoe collection.

With its reliance on catchy beats to liven up history, there are echoes of Hamilton as well as Six, the Broadway hit about Henry VIII’s wives that culminates in a long-awaited rise-from-your-seats dance party. But Here Lies Love, which melds dirty dancing with dirty politics, rouses audience members from the jump.
It’s an experience unlike any other you’ve ever had on Broadway.

Our complicity with such cycles of populist fervor—whether, depending on your ticket, as spectators from a safe distance or as extras in a mob scene—is the loudly beating heart of Here Lies Love, a party that hides a mordant critique of civilization and its discotheques.
The show succeeds in making the audience complicit in the Marcoses' rise to power, forcing us to reckon with our own susceptibility to charismatic authoritarianism.
Perhaps that’s why Here Lies Love, for all its impressive confidence, feels a bit thin in afterthought.
David Byrne's immersive disco musical about Imelda Marcos is a knockout that turns Broadway into a dance floor.
It’s an irrefutably great time — one that rivals the Hell’s Kitchen clubs mere blocks away — even as the weight of autocratic abuse hovers just above the lustered air.
The immersive staging of 'Here Lies Love' transforms the Broadway Theatre into a glittering nightclub where audiences dance alongside performers in this musical about Imelda Marcos.

That she would probably adore the over-emphatic atmosphere of “Here Lies Love” — with its lurid lighting by Justin Townsend, skittering projections by Peter Nigrini and earsplitting sound by M.L. Dogg and Cody Spencer — is, however, equivocal praise.
But glorifying its subject is an uneasy proposition that the production hasn't managed to reconcile.
The show as a whole may have wobbled from such instability, but at least for Ireland the resulting flexibility made her Sonya into something I’d never seen before.
It’s a stunningly effective moment, contrasting the dazzlingly theatrical show that precedes it.

Here Lies Love is nonetheless an 'event,' and given its easily digestible score, its historical pertinence, its abounding energy, and its unforgettable ambience, I think it's going to be loved for quite a while.
By any measure, Here Lies Love is a perfectly crafted, thrilling production that should make audiences very happy indeed.
Bravo to a Broadway show that's willing to ask such big questions in such an entertaining way.
This rollicking, form-breaking musical party is well worth an RSVP.

Arriving at the Broadway Theatre, Here Lies Love proves itself more than a gimmick, or an Obama-era flash in the pan: it’s a spectacular look at celebrity, vanity, and power, undergirded by a nonstop parade of danceable, singable hits.

Besides the great songs, with music by Byrne and Fatboy Slim and lyrics by Byrne - the alluring title number might become permanently lodged in your brain - there's inventive choreography by Annie-B Parson, eye-catching, quick-change costumes designed by Clint Ramos, Justin Townsend's atmospheric lighting scheme and David Korins' remarkably engi...
It's an important history lesson, an innovative use of theater space, and a disco dance party, all at once.
That’s the genius of Here Lies Love, which premiered in a much more intimate production at the Public Theater in 2013.

Here Lies Love remains an impressive and effective experience; but uptown on Broadway, at the over-sized Broadway, the bloom is off the rose of Tacloban (to borrow the title of Imelda’s opening number).
The lack of live music remains a stain on an otherwise remarkable show.
Here Lies Love is a show that succeeds most when it remembers that nightclub-style entertainment is supposed to be, above all else, entertaining
Alex Timbers' extraordinarily inventive direction makes this musical worth seeing.
When I saw audience members decked out in their sequins and ready for a night on the town on the dance floor, I felt like maybe the shows messaging was more opaque than I had appreciated.
"Some have complained that Here Lies Love glamorizes the Marcoses, an argument that is hard to credit, especially when their crimes pile up during the show's second half.
That’s both a compliment and a critique, as Alex Timbers’ multimedia treatment is so heavy on spectacle it makes “Moulin Rouge” (another Timbers production) seem simple by comparison.
Each of the three aspects offers its own pleasures, even as each has its own shortcomings, and together they sometimes work at cross purposes.
Here Lies Love unreels like an MTV music video with the emotional content lost in the technique.
The musical sings and dances up a storm, while not making much of a case there is anything to sing and dance about.

Visitors were given the impression that they had arrived at a hopping discotec in downtown Manila, where the narrative took place. From a platform above, an aviators-clad DJ announced that visitors of “Club Millennium” were obligated to dance.
The Marcos family is back in power, and it is both profound and intensely disturbing to realize that we are here dancing about it, clapping along, pretending all that matters is love.
It is an immersive spectacle that is almost guaranteed to impress.
Here Lies Love'' works as a spectacle and participatory theater.

The historic all-Filipino cast is a powerhouse. All in all, this production exposes the need for more Filipino stories written by Filipinos that center the survivors of the continuous impact of the Marcos family. While the show succinctly highlights Imelda’s cruelty, the hour and a half time constraint reduces the topic’s complexities.
Here Lies Love is a history lesson wrapped in a tale of broken hearts and presented as engaging songs.
You can still feel the multi-layered invention on parade, and it’s often breathtaking.

cn.t: Critics praise this immersive disco musical's innovative staging and all-Filipino cast, though some question whether its catchy, dance-party format adequately grapples with the Marcos regime's darker historical complexities.

sg.ra: The Broadway Theatre is a 1924 column-free house — Wikipedia notes the balcony is carried by a 40-ton girder 'supported solely by the side walls,' which eliminates the pillar problems that plague older big Shubert houses of this size. That makes center orchestra D-G genuinely safer than at most 1,700+ seat theatres: no interior posts to work around. Multiple guides converge on rows D-G, seats 105-109, as the premium sweet spot, and center orchestra row G seat 105 was reviewed simply as 'Center orchestra. What could be better?'. Caveat for this specific house: the orchestra pit sits between row A and the stage, and reviewers consistently report the stage is unusually high — front-row patrons 'can't see feet' and crane their neck. D-G hits the first row where eyeline clears cleanly, well ahead of the mezzanine overhang at row J-K.

sg.n: Orchestra Left / Right Mid (Rows C-L, side blocks)
sg.ra: The Broadway Theatre's orchestra side blocks (Left even-numbered, Right odd-numbered) sit at a sharp angle because the house is unusually wide — 46'6" proscenium in a ~909-seat orchestra. Far-aisle seats past double-digits (14+) get the worst of the angle: one Gatsby reviewer in Orchestra L row B seat 10 warned 'restricted view, missed basically all action at the back of the stage, as well as the grandeur of the set itself.' The mid-range (rows C-L, seats up to low teens) is a real $50-cheaper alternative to center — Orchestra L row E seat 2: 'This seat is like $50 cheaper than center orchestra. You can still see everything and since you're on the aisle you don't have to worry about a head getting in the way.' Row E is called out specifically as close enough for facial expressions with no obstruction.

This is the single most-warned-about zone at the Broadway Theatre because of its unusual geometry: above you sits the cantilevered 1675 Broadway office tower, and the mezzanine overhang drops hard over the rear orchestra. Per AViewFromMySeat Orchestra R row U seat 13: 'theres a bit of a balcony overhang that blocks the view at the top of the stage.' Row T's own SneakyBeagle agreed. One Miss Saigon reviewer in Orchestra R row T seat 23 was blunt: 'felt very far back, mezzanine overhang gave an odd feeling of separation from the action onstage. Would recommend a closer seat or something in the mezzanine.' In a house this size, the smarter move is a rear-mezzanine row A-B at similar price — you get elevation instead of being crushed under the overhang.

The Broadway Theatre's front mezzanine is the smallest section in the house (only 250 seats across 6 rows A-F) and sits very close to the stage because the single-balcony construction means no upper balcony above it — 'No overhang from Rear Mezzanine' per SeatPlan, a structural feature you don't get in most big Broadway houses with two-tier balconies. Reviewers repeatedly call Front Mezz LC/RC A-C 'some of the best seats in this theatre' (AbbeySouth44), and for spectacle shows with vertical staging the overhead angle is actively preferred — a West Side Story reviewer specifically said 'Best to see this show in Mezz to see video portion of the set. Front orchestra would miss action.' The row A safety railing can cut into sightlines for shorter patrons so row B is the safer pick.

Front Mezz L/R at the Broadway Theatre is the sleeper-comfort pick in the building because of one very specific quirk: the far ends of row A 'flare out' where the row meets the aisle, creating outsized legroom. An AVFMS reviewer in Front Mezzanine L row A seat 16 says it plainly: 'This seat probably has the most legroom in the whole theatre! Because it's on the edge of the row where it flares out, you can fully straighten your legs! The lefthand corner of the stage is slightly obscured by the railing, but it's so worth it.' Trade-off is a slightly cut stage-corner and the usual side angle, but for 6'+ patrons in a house whose mid-rows are repeatedly called 'tight', this is an actual workaround rather than a marketing claim.

Rear Mezzanine Center row A-C is the Broadway Theatre's signature value play because of a layout feature specific to this house: the rear mezzanine is 'elevated above the Front Mezzanine' with a horizontal aisle dividing the two, and row A of the rear mezz has that aisle directly in front — so no heads block sightlines in the first rear-mezz row. AViewFromMySeat user in RC row A seat 111 confirmed: 'theres an aisle in front of the seats so no heads are in front of you.' Combined with the column-free engineering, center-A is an unobstructed elevated center-perspective at rear-mezz prices — one 123LGB reviewer: 'Looks far in the photo but it felt closer. Good sightlines.' Caveats: one 6'2" reviewer called RC row A seat 111 'agony' — railing sits at knee height — so book further back if you're tall.

Rear Mezzanine at the Broadway Theatre runs A-R (an unusually deep balcony — 584 seats alone, larger than many full Broadway houses), and SeatPlan warns views become 'less reliable' beyond row J with the back quarter feeling 'very distant.' Side blocks (Rear Mezzanine L, Rear Mezzanine R rows E-R) compound distance with angle — one Great Gatsby reviewer in Rear Mezzanine LC row E seat 122 confirmed 'Good view of the stage, but was very far away,' and E seat 11 reviewer: 'No obstructions though you do feel the distance between the stage. Cannot see facial expressions.' In a house already 900+ seats deep in the orchestra, combining side-angle with deep balcony distance is the worst combination of hazards offered here.
